title: A Strong Start, an Unfinished Task
overview: After Joshua dies, Israel's tribes fight to settle the land, and Judah's early victories give way to a long list of towns they never took.

parts.label: Judah goes first (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: With no leader to replace Joshua, the tribes ask the LORD who should lead, and Judah, the largest tribe, is chosen and teams up with the small neighboring tribe of Simeon. They cut off the captured king Adoni-Bezek's thumbs and big toes so he could never fight again, and he calls it payback for doing the same to seventy local rulers.

parts.label: Jerusalem, Hebron and Debir (vv. 8-15)
parts.note: Judah burns Jerusalem and takes Hebron and Debir, though verse 21 says Jerusalem was still not fully taken, a tension scholars have long noted. Caleb offers his daughter in marriage as a reward for capturing Debir, and she boldly asks him for springs, because her dry southern land was worth little without water.

parts.label: Judah's wider campaign (vv. 16-21)
parts.note: The Kenites, relatives of Moses by marriage, go up with Judah to settle near Arad, while Judah and Simeon wipe out the town of Zephath and rename it Hormah, which sounds like the Hebrew word for destruction. Judah holds the hills but not the plains, where chariots fitted with iron gave the locals the edge, and Benjamin fails to take Jerusalem.

parts.label: Bethel taken by betrayal (vv. 22-26)
parts.note: Spies promise a local man safety if he shows them a way into the city, and the city is then put to the sword. He and his family are spared and go off to found a new town with the city's old name, Luz.

parts.label: Tribes that fell short (vv. 27-36)
parts.note: Tribe after tribe leaves Canaanite towns standing, sometimes forcing the people into labor instead of driving them out. The list reads like a slide from victory into compromise, which the next chapter and the rest of the book treat as a root of Israel's later troubles.

disagreement: Christians differ on why the tribes fell short, some reading it mainly as a failure of trust and obedience toward God, and others reading verses like 19 as a plain report of real military limits that the writer does not blame on anyone.
think: When a group starts out united and determined, what do you think leads it, over time, to settle for good enough?
